title: Why Chanel No. 5 is No. 5
hook: The world's most famous perfume is named after a sample number.
peek: In 1920 Coco Chanel sniffed a set of trial perfumes made for her by the perfumer Ernest Beaux. She picked the vial labelled 5 and simply kept the label, giving the scent one of the plainest names in fashion.
lede: In 1920 Coco Chanel asked the perfumer Ernest Beaux to make her a new scent. Working in Grasse, in the south of France, he prepared a series of samples in small numbered vials. Chanel tried them and chose the one marked 5. Rather than give it a romantic name, as perfumes usually had, she kept the number. Chanel No. 5 launched in 1921.

bullets.text: The trial vials are usually described as two series, numbered 1 to 5 and 20 to 24. Beaux had earlier worked as a perfumer in Moscow, and he built No. 5 from an idea he had been developing there.

Chanel is said to have thought of five as her lucky number, and the story goes that she presented the perfume on the fifth day of the fifth month. These details come from later retellings and are hard to confirm.
No. 5 was one of the first perfumes to use a large dose of synthetic chemicals called aldehydes. They give a bright, fizzy lift to the top of the scent, so it smells of no single flower.
The bottle was a simple rectangle with a black-and-white label, closer to a chemist's flask than the ornate bottles of the day. Its shape has changed only slightly in a century.
In a 1952 magazine interview, Marilyn Monroe was asked what she wore to bed and answered that she wore Chanel No. 5. The line became one of the most quoted pieces of perfume publicity ever.
